evidence: Area A carries the highest syllabus weight (30–40%) and 69 examiner observations sit in it; 17 banked questions map to this chapter's subtopics, 3 of them in the two 2025 BIA papers. A question can map to more than one subtopic, so counts overlap across chapters.
key_points: External environment and why it is scanned
Spectrum of political ideologies and their business impact
Social environment and its influence on business
label: learn
summary: The outside world a business cannot control, seen through three lenses: politics — who governs, what they believe and how policy shifts bite; economics — where the economy sits in its cycle and what indicators like inflation and interest rates are signalling; and society — demographics, culture and attitudes. The examinable skill is not reciting ideology definitions but tracing how a political or economic change alters one specific business's prospects.
title: PESTEL analysis (I) — Political, economic and social environment

evidence: Area A weight 30–40%; 15 banked questions map to technological disruption, 2 in the 2025 papers. A question can map to more than one subtopic, so counts overlap across chapters.
key_points: Impact of technological change on working methods
Technological disruption and the business environment
label: learn
summary: The other three PESTEL lenses: how technology changes working methods and disrupts whole industries, how ecological pressures — climate, resources, regulation — constrain what businesses can do, and how the legal framework sets the rules of the game. The disruption case studies show the pattern examiners reward: incumbents that adapt survive, those that do not fade.
title: PESTEL analysis (II) — Technological, ecological and legal environment

evidence: Practice chapter: no new theory and no standalone subtopic — its cases draw on Chapters 1–2, so no banked questions count here separately. Its value is working the cases, not memorising content.
key_points: Spotting the factors that matter in a scenario
label: understand
summary: No new theory — worked PESTEL cases with model answers, including a technology manufacturer weighing a new market. Its job is exam technique: spotting which PESTEL factors actually matter in a scenario, linking each one to the business in front of you, and structuring an answer that argues rather than lists.
title: PESTEL analysis (III) — Case study questions

evidence: 21 banked questions map here, 8 in the 2025 papers — the most of any Area A subtopic; 69 examiner observations sit in Area A. A question can map to more than one subtopic, so counts overlap across chapters.
key_points: Strategic groups, segmentation and the BCG matrix
label: learn
summary: How to judge whether an industry is worth being in and where a firm stands inside it: the five forces that squeeze profits, where a product sits in its life cycle, how firms cluster into strategic groups, and how the BCG matrix sorts a portfolio into stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs.
title: Competitive forces

evidence: 37 banked questions map here, 12 in the 2025 papers — the largest footprint of any chapter; internal analysis dominates Area A. A question can map to more than one subtopic, so counts overlap across chapters.
key_points: Customer needs and critical success factors
Porter's value chain and SWOT analysis
label: learn
summary: Looking inside the firm: what it is actually good at (resources and competences), whether that advantage will last, what its customers really need, and where the value chain shows value being created or lost — pulled together into a SWOT that faces both ways, inward and outward.
title: Internal analysis

evidence: 13 banked questions map here (3 in the 2025 papers). Short, purely conceptual chapter: frameworks to apply to scenarios, not calculations to drill — grasp and apply rather than master in depth.
key_points: Nature of ethics and business ethics
Applying a framework to a dilemma
label: understand
summary: How to decide when the right answer is not obvious: the chapter sets out step-by-step ethical frameworks — models that test a decision against stakeholders, duties and consequences — and applies them to business dilemmas. Short and conceptual: learn the models well enough to run one on an unseen scenario.
title: Ethical decision making models

evidence: Brand-new 2025-scheme area (weight 10–15%, the lowest); all 12 banked questions come from the two 2025 papers and only 3 examiner observations touch it — past evidence is thin, so the depth examiners will go to is hard to predict. Learn the concepts; do not skip it.
key_points: Measuring corporate sustainability: the ESG framework
label: understand
summary: The syllabus's newest area: what sustainability means beyond slogans, who the stakeholders are, how the economic, social and environmental pillars connect, and how ESG measures try to score corporate sustainability. The concepts are new to the exam, so past papers show the direction but not the full depth.
title: Introduction to sustainability

evidence: 29 banked questions map here, 7 in the 2025 papers; Area B weight 20–30% with 52 examiner observations. A question can map to more than one subtopic, so counts overlap across chapters.
key_points: Islamic finance and other common sources
label: learn
summary: How companies raise money: shares, loans, retained profits and Islamic alternatives — and the trade-offs that drive the choice for a given business: cost, control, risk and availability. The chapter builds the vocabulary every later finance question assumes.
title: Sources of finance

evidence: 27 banked questions map here, 9 in the 2025 papers; WACC and CAPM are the calculation core of Area B. A question can map to more than one subtopic, so counts overlap across chapters.
key_points: Cost of equity and cost of debt
Valuation of debts and yield curves
label: learn
summary: The price of money: what return shareholders and lenders demand, how to blend them into a weighted average cost of capital, and how bond values and yield curves reflect risk and rates. This is the calculation core of Area B — WACC and CAPM questions reward careful workings, not memorised answers.
title: Cost of finance

evidence: 39 banked questions map here, 9 in the 2025 papers — the largest footprint in Area B. A question can map to more than one subtopic, so counts overlap across chapters.
key_points: Types of financial risk and their management
label: learn
summary: How firms handle risks they cannot avoid: the ISO 31000 process — identify, assess, treat, monitor — and the financial toolkit for hedging interest-rate, currency and commodity exposure with forwards, futures and options. The most question-heavy chapter in Area B.
title: Financial risk management

evidence: 19 banked questions map here (2 in the 2025 papers); Area C weight 25–30% with 65 examiner observations. A question can map to more than one subtopic, so counts overlap across chapters.
key_points: Budgeting in non-profits and human aspects
label: learn
summary: Turning plans into numbers: what budgets are for, the types (fixed, flexible, rolling, zero-based and others), how to build them, and the human side — why budgets motivate or demotivate the people who live under them.
title: Budgeting

evidence: 14 banked questions map here (2 in the 2025 papers); Area C weight 25–30% with 65 examiner observations. A question can map to more than one subtopic, so counts overlap across chapters.
label: learn
summary: The day-to-day money engine: how much working capital a business needs, how to fund it, and how managing debtors and creditors — terms, discounts, chasing — frees cash or traps it. Compact chapter, directly applicable to case questions.
title: Working capital management

evidence: 11 banked questions map here (3 in the 2025 papers); NPV and IRR are core calculation skills in Area C. A question can map to more than one subtopic, so counts overlap across chapters.
key_points: Net present value and internal rate of return
Asset replacement cycle and capital rationing
label: learn
summary: Whether a long-term investment is worth it: payback for speed, then discounted methods — net present value and internal rate of return — with the complications of inflation, tax, replacing assets and choosing between projects when capital is rationed.
title: Introduction to project appraisal
